stem: During a crown prep, spatter from the patient's mouth strikes an assistant in the eye because she forgot her protective eyewear. Which mode of transmission does this represent?
choices: Indirect contact with a contaminated surface
Inhalation of airborne microorganisms
Droplet contact with a mucous membrane
Percutaneous injury from a sharp instrument
explanation: Spatter is made of droplets propelled a short distance, and the eye's conjunctiva is a mucous membrane, so this is droplet contact with mucosa. It is not airborne inhalation, which involves tiny particles that stay suspended and are breathed in.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Background
source_quote: contact of conjunctival, nasal, or oral mucosa with droplets (e.g., spatter) containing microorganisms generated from an infected person and propelled a short distance

subtopic: I.A chain of infection and occupational risk
stem: An assistant with confirmed immunity to hepatitis B sustains a needlestick from a patient who has chronic HBV infection. Which link in the chain of infection is missing, making infection unlikely?
choices: A susceptible host
A portal of entry
A mode of transmission
A reservoir for the pathogen
explanation: Infection requires a susceptible host, meaning a person who is not immune, and this assistant is immune. The needlestick still provides a portal of entry and a mode of transmission, so those links are present.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Background (chain of infection)
source_quote: a portal of entry through which the pathogen can enter the host; and a susceptible host (i.e., one who is not immune).

stem: How is hepatitis B virus (HBV) transmitted to dental health care personnel?
choices: Casual contact such as shaking hands with an infected patient
Breathing the same room air as an infected patient
Touching intact skin that has been in contact with saliva
Percutaneous or mucosal exposure to blood or body fluids
explanation: HBV spreads when infected blood or body fluids get through the skin (such as a needlestick) or onto a mucous membrane. It is a bloodborne virus, not an airborne one, so shared room air is not the route.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Hepatitis B Virus
source_quote: HBV is transmitted by percutaneous or mucosal exposure to blood or body fluids of a person with either acute or chronic HBV infection.

subtopic: I.B medical history and Standard Precautions
stem: A new patient's completed health history lists no infectious diseases of any kind. What level of infection prevention should the team use for this patient's treatment?
choices: Reduced precautions, since no infection was reported
Standard Precautions, the same as for every patient
Transmission-Based Precautions until lab tests confirm status
Standard Precautions only if bleeding is expected
explanation: Standard Precautions apply to all patient care regardless of whether an infection is suspected or confirmed, because a health history cannot identify every infected patient. Transmission-Based Precautions are an added tier for known or suspected contact, droplet, or airborne diseases, not a default for unknowns.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Standard Precautions
source_quote: Standard Precautions are the minimum infection prevention practices that apply to all patient care, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status of the patient, in any setting where health care is delivered.

stem: While reviewing a patient's medical history, the assistant sees a documented latex allergy. Which scheduling choice best reduces the patient's exposure to airborne latex particles?
choices: The last appointment of the day, after the operatory is cleaned
Any open appointment, as long as nitrile gloves are worn
The first appointment of the day
A midday appointment, after the morning air has cleared
explanation: Scheduling a latex-allergic patient first in the day minimizes contact with latex particles that build up in the air during the day. Wearing nitrile gloves helps, but it does not address latex allergens already in the ambient air from earlier patients.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Contact Dermatitis and Latex Hypersensitivity
source_quote: Patients with latex allergy can be scheduled for the first appointment of the day to minimize their inadvertent exposure to airborne latex particles.

stem: After removing her gloves, an assistant notices a smear of the patient's blood on her wrist. Which hand hygiene method should she use?
choices: Wash with soap and water
Apply an alcohol-based hand rub
Apply an alcohol-based hand rub twice
Wipe with a surface disinfectant towelette
explanation: When hands are visibly soiled with blood or body fluids, use soap and water. Alcohol-based hand rubs are fine for hands that are not visibly soiled, but repeating the rub does not make it the right choice here.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Hand Hygiene, Key Recommendations
source_quote: Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled (e.g., blood, body fluids); otherwise, an alcohol-based hand rub may be used.

stem: An assistant with dry, cracked hands wants to use a petroleum-based hand lotion. When is it appropriate for her to apply it?
choices: Right before gloving each morning, to prevent dermatitis
After each handwashing between patients
During the lunch break, before afternoon patients
Only at the end of the work day
explanation: Petroleum and other oil emollients can weaken latex gloves and make them more permeable, so these lotions should be used only at the end of the work day. A lunch break application is tempting, but the lotion would still be on her hands under afternoon gloves.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Hand Hygiene, Lotions
source_quote: For that reason, lotions that contain petroleum or other oil emollients should only be used at the end of the work day

stem: Which fingernail practice is recommended for dental health care personnel?
choices: Nails long enough to protect fingertips during glove changes
Nails kept short with smooth, filed edges
Nails of any length if sealed with clear polish
Short natural nails reinforced with artificial tips
explanation: Short nails with smooth, filed edges can be cleaned thoroughly and are less likely to tear gloves. Artificial nails and extenders carry more bacteria and are generally not recommended, even over short natural nails.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), Recommendations: Special Considerations for Hand Hygiene and Glove Use
source_quote: Keep fingernails short with smooth, filed edges to allow thorough cleaning and prevent glove tears

stem: An assistant is removing and disposing of her PPE after a procedure. What is always the final step?
choices: Removing the protective gown
Removing the mask by its ties or ear loops
Performing hand hygiene
Wiping down the protective eyewear
explanation: Hand hygiene is always the last step after PPE is removed and discarded, because hands can pick up contamination while taking PPE off. The mask and gown come off before that final step, not after it.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), section: Personal Protective Equipment
source_quote: DHCP should be trained to select and put on appropriate PPE and remove PPE so that the chance for skin or clothing contamination is reduced. Hand hygiene is always the final step after removing and disposing of PPE.

subtopic: I.D preparing reusable PPE and patient protection
stem: At the end of an appointment, the patient's reusable protective eyewear shows no visible soil. How should the assistant prepare it for the next patient?
choices: Clean it with soap and water
Run it through a steam sterilizer cycle
Reuse it as is, since it is not visibly soiled
Discard it and open a new pair
explanation: Reusable facial protective equipment, including patient eyewear, is cleaned with soap and water between patients, and also disinfected when visibly soiled. Skipping cleaning because nothing is visible is wrong, since cleaning between patients is required either way.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), Recommendations: PPE, Masks, Protective Eyewear, and Face Shields
source_quote: Clean with soap and water, or if visibly soiled, clean and disinfect reusable facial protective equipment (e.g., clinician and patient protective eyewear or face shields) between patients

stem: Midway through placing a matrix band, an assistant notices a small tear in her glove. What should she do?
choices: Put a new glove on over the torn one and keep working
Wipe the torn glove with alcohol and finish the step
Finish the procedure, then change gloves before the next patient
Remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene, then put on new gloves
explanation: Torn, cut, or punctured gloves are removed, hands are cleaned, and new gloves are put on. Layering a new glove over the torn one leaves possibly contaminated skin underneath without hand hygiene.
source_citation: CDC, Summary of Infection Prevention Practices in Dental Settings (2016), Appendix A Checklist, II.2 Personal Protective Equipment, Gloves
source_quote: DHCP remove gloves that are torn, cut, or punctured and perform hand hygiene before putting on new gloves

stem: An assistant's protective lab coat is splattered with blood during a procedure. Under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, who is responsible for laundering it?
choices: The assistant, who should wash it at home in hot water
The employer, at no cost to the employee
The assistant, using a commercial service she pays for
Whoever the office manager assigns that week
explanation: OSHA requires the employer to clean, launder, and dispose of required PPE at no cost to the employee. Laundering is the employer's job, so the assistant should not be washing it at home or paying for cleaning herself.
source_quote: The employer shall clean, launder, and dispose of personal protective equipment required by paragraphs (d) and (e) of this standard, at no cost to the employee.

stem: A hygienist working without an assistant is about to use an ultrasonic scaler. A dental dam cannot be placed for this procedure. Which added step best reduces the microorganisms in the aerosol and spatter she generates?
choices: Place cotton rolls in the vestibules before scaling
Raise the water flow to the scaler tip
Have the patient use an antimicrobial preprocedural rinse
Use a saliva ejector in place of evacuation
explanation: An antimicrobial preprocedural rinse lowers the level of oral microorganisms in aerosols and spatter, and it is most useful for scaling and polishing, where a dental dam cannot be used and solo providers rarely use high-volume evacuation. Cotton rolls and a saliva ejector manage fluid but do not reduce the microbial load of the spray.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Preprocedural Mouth Rinses
source_quote: Preprocedural mouth rinses can be most beneficial before a procedure that requires using a prophylaxis cup or ultrasonic scaler because rubber dams cannot be used to minimize aerosol and spatter generation and, unless the provider has an assistant, high-volume evacuation is not commonly used

stem: The visible spray produced by a high-speed handpiece or air-water syringe is made up mostly of what?
choices: Large-particle droplets of water, saliva, blood, and debris
Respirable aerosols that stay airborne for hours
Droplet nuclei small enough to pass through a surgical mask
Vaporized chemicals from the dental unit waterline
explanation: The visible spray is mainly large-particle spatter that travels a short distance and settles quickly onto nearby surfaces, people, and the floor. It may contain some aerosols, but they are not the bulk of the spray.
source_citation: CDC, Guidelines for Infection Control in Dental Health-Care Settings (2003), section: Personal Protective Equipment
source_quote: Use of rotary dental and surgical instruments (e.g., handpieces or ultrasonic scalers) and air-water syringes creates a visible spray that contains primarily large-particle droplets of water, saliva, blood, microorganisms, and other debris.
